content: 1. Both ginger and Panax ginseng have anticoagulant properties, which may increase the risk of bleeding. It is essential to use these substances with caution and monitor the patient closely. 2. The combination of parecoxib and ginger can enhance anticoagulation effects. Careful monitoring is advised to prevent potential complications. 3. Ginger and pau d'arco both exhibit anticoagulant effects. Their concurrent use requires caution and close monitoring to mitigate bleeding risks. 4. Phenindione and ginger together can significantly increase anticoagulation. Therapy adjustments may be necessary, and close monitoring is strongly recommended. 5. Ginger and phytoestrogens both enhance anticoagulation. Use these substances cautiously and monitor the patient closely. 6. Piroxicam and ginger, when used together, can increase anticoagulation. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 7. The combination of ginger and prasugrel may exhibit pharmacodynamic synergy, potentially prolonging bleeding time. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, and conflicting evidence exists. Use with caution and monitor closely. 8. Protamine and ginger both increase anticoagulation. Therapy modifications may be required, and close monitoring is essential. 9. Ginger and reishi mushroom both enhance anticoagulation. Their combined use necessitates caution and close monitoring. 10. Reteplase and ginger together can increase anticoagulation. Therapy adjustments may be needed, and close monitoring is crucial. 11. Non-aspirin salicylates and ginger both enhance anticoagulation. Use with caution and monitor the patient closely. 12. Salsalate and ginger, when used together, can increase anticoagulation. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 13. Ginger and Siberian ginseng both enhance anticoagulation. Their concurrent use requires caution and close monitoring. 14. Sulfasalazine and ginger both increase anticoagulation. Use these substances cautiously and monitor the patient closely. 15. Sulindac and ginger, when used together, can enhance anticoagulation. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 16. Tenecteplase and ginger together can significantly increase anticoagulation. Therapy modifications may be required, and close monitoring is essential. 17. The combination of ginger and ticlopidine may exhibit pharmacodynamic synergy, potentially prolonging bleeding time. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, and conflicting evidence exists. Use with caution and monitor closely. 18. Ginger and tirofiban may have pharmacodynamic synergy, potentially increasing bleeding time. The clinical significance of this interaction is uncertain, and evidence is conflicting. Use cautiously and monitor closely. 19. Tolfenamic acid and ginger both enhance anticoagulation. Their concurrent use requires caution and close monitoring. 20. Tolmetin and ginger, when used together, can increase anticoagulation. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 21. Ginger increases anticoagulation, while vitamin K1 (phytomenadione) decreases it. The net effect of this interaction is unclear. Use with caution and monitor the patient closely. 22. Ginger may increase the tendency for bleeding and cause side effects such as abdominal discomfort, cardiac arrhythmias (in overdose), central nervous system depression (in overdose), dermatitis (with topical use), diarrhea, heartburn, and mouth or throat irritation. Hypersensitivity reactions and gallbladder disease may also occur. 23. Patients with bleeding disorders, cardiac disease, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, or hypotension should use ginger cautiously. 24. During pregnancy, ginger is not recommended by the German Commission E. However, current data suggest it is safe when used at usual therapeutic doses. 25. Regarding lactation, there is no available data (N/A). 26. Ginger is generally considered acceptable (Category A) during pregnancy. Controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk.
